*Originally November 4, 2026; expanded November 27, 2026.*

*This post is generated by ChatGPT based on my discussions with it. It is a bit too tedious to write all these results and proofs out by myself.*

The issue I want to remember is the distinction between taking the limsup of random variables, taking the limsup of events, and taking the limsup of their probabilities. These are three different operations. The strict and weak inequalities matter a lot here, especially at the boundary of a threshold.

## 1. All the main limsup results first

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, let $(Y_n)_{n\geq1}$ be any sequence of real-valued random variables, and fix $x\in\mathbb R$. Write

$$
L:=\limsup_{n\to\infty}Y_n
=\inf_{N\geq1}\sup_{n\geq N}Y_n.
$$

Here $L$ is an extended real-valued measurable function. No independence, integrability or convergence assumptions are needed.

### Four possible events involving strict and weak upper thresholds

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{L>x\}
&\subseteq\limsup_n\{Y_n>x\}\\
&\subseteq\limsup_n\{Y_n\geq x\}\\
&\subseteq\{L\geq x\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

All three inclusions can be strict. In particular, neither of the two set-theoretic limsups is generally equal to the corresponding event involving the numerical limsup.

### Probability inequalities

By monotonicity of probability,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(L\geq x)
&\geq P(\limsup_n\{Y_n\geq x\})\\
&\geq P(\limsup_n\{Y_n>x\})\\
&\geq P(L>x).
\end{aligned}
$$

By reverse Fatou's lemma, for every sequence of events $A_n\in\mathcal F$,

$$
\boxed{P(\limsup_n A_n)\geq\limsup_n P(A_n).}
$$

Combining the results for weak thresholds gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(L\geq x)
&\geq P(\limsup_n\{Y_n\geq x\})\\
&\geq\limsup_n P(Y_n\geq x),
\end{aligned}
$$

and for strict thresholds,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(L\geq x)
&\geq P(\limsup_n\{Y_n>x\})\\
&\geq\limsup_n P(Y_n>x).
\end{aligned}
$$

Also,

$$
\limsup_n P(Y_n\geq x)
\geq\limsup_n P(Y_n>x).
$$

The important warning is that in both three-term probability chains, the numerical limsup event on the left uses $\geq$, even when the marginal probabilities on the right use $>$. In general, neither direction of inequality holds between $P(L>x)$ and $\limsup_n P(Y_n>x)$; the same warning holds for $\limsup_n P(Y_n\geq x)$.

### Adjusting the threshold

For any $x'<x$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{L>x\}
&\subseteq\limsup_n\{Y_n>x\}\\
&\subseteq\limsup_n\{Y_n\geq x\}\\
&\subseteq\{L\geq x\}\\
&\subseteq\{L>x'\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is particularly useful when the assertion in question is quantified over every positive threshold.

## 2. The underlying logic of sup and inf

The subtlety in all these results comes from some elementary real analysis. It is worth writing all the logical relationships out explicitly.

Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty, $k\in\mathbb R$, and take the supremum and infimum in the extended real line.

### Existential quantification

For sup:

$$
\sup S>k
\iff
\exists s\in S:\ s>k.
$$

But

$$
\sup S\geq k
\impliedby
\exists s\in S:\ s\geq k,
$$

and the reverse implication is not generally true.

For inf:

$$
\inf S<k
\iff
\exists s\in S:\ s<k.
$$

But

$$
\inf S\leq k
\impliedby
\exists s\in S:\ s\leq k,
$$

and the reverse implication is not generally true.

### Universal quantification

For sup:

$$
\sup S\leq k
\iff
\forall s\in S,\ s\leq k.
$$

But

$$
\sup S<k
\implies
\forall s\in S,\ s<k,
$$

and the reverse implication is not generally true.

For inf:

$$
\inf S\geq k
\iff
\forall s\in S,\ s\geq k.
$$

But

$$
\inf S>k
\implies
\forall s\in S,\ s>k,
$$

and the reverse implication is not generally true.

### Why the strict/weak distinction?

Consider the set

$$
S_-=\{k-1/n:n\geq1\}.
$$

Every element of $S_-$ is strictly less than $k$, but $\sup S_-=k$. So the supremum is not attained. This simultaneously shows that

- $\sup S\geq k$ need not imply that there exists an element $s\geq k$;
- all elements being strictly less than $k$ need not imply $\sup S<k$.

Similarly, consider

$$
S_+=\{k+1/n:n\geq1\}.
$$

Every element is strictly greater than $k$, but $\inf S_+=k$. This shows that

- $\inf S\leq k$ need not imply that there exists an element $s\leq k$;
- all elements being strictly greater than $k$ need not imply $\inf S>k$.

The true equivalences follow directly from the least-upper-bound and greatest-lower-bound properties. For instance, if $\sup S>k$ but no element is strictly greater than $k$, then $k$ would be an upper bound, a contradiction. Conversely, if some $s>k$, then $\sup S\geq s>k$. The other equivalences follow in the same way or by negating the corresponding statements.

If we want an equivalence involving an infimum strictly greater than $k$ and universal quantification, we need a uniform margin:

$$
\inf S>k
\iff
\exists\delta>0,\ \forall s\in S,\
s\geq k+\delta.
$$

Similarly,

$$
\sup S<k
\iff
\exists\delta>0,\ \forall s\in S,\
s\leq k-\delta.
$$

**Memory rule:** existential quantification with a strict inequality, universal quantification with a weak inequality. These are the combinations giving equivalences in the appropriate sup/inf direction. For the other combinations, pay attention to which implication survives.

## 3. Proof of the four-event chain

Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
B_x&=\{L>x\},\\
A_x&=\limsup_n\{Y_n>x\},\\
D_x&=\limsup_n\{Y_n\geq x\},\\
C_x&=\{L\geq x\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Fix $\omega\in\Omega$ throughout. Suppress $\omega$ in the notation for the numerical values $Y_n(\omega)$.

First, $\omega\in B_x$ means

$$
\inf_{N\geq1}\sup_{n\geq N}Y_n>x.
$$

This implies

$$
\forall N\geq1,\quad
\sup_{n\geq N}Y_n>x.
$$

By the sup/inf logic above, this is equivalent to

$$
\forall N\geq1,\ \exists n\geq N:
Y_n>x.
$$

This is precisely the definition of $\omega\in A_x$. Thus $B_x\subseteq A_x$.

The important point is that the very first implication is not reversible: each tail supremum being strictly greater than $x$ does not guarantee their infimum is strictly greater than $x$.

The inclusion $A_x\subseteq D_x$ is immediate, since $Y_n>x$ implies $Y_n\geq x$ for every index.

Finally, $\omega\in D_x$ means

$$
\forall N\geq1,\ \exists n\geq N:
Y_n\geq x.
$$

This implies

$$
\forall N\geq1,\quad
\sup_{n\geq N}Y_n\geq x.
$$

Taking the infimum over $N$ preserves the weak inequality:

$$
\inf_{N\geq1}\sup_{n\geq N}Y_n\geq x.
$$

Hence $D_x\subseteq C_x$.

Here the problematic reverse step is the one involving the supremum: a supremum greater than or equal to $x$ need not be attained at a term greater than or equal to $x$.

Putting everything together,

$$
\boxed{B_x\subseteq A_x\subseteq D_x\subseteq C_x.}
$$

### Why none of the three inclusions is reversible

These examples work even with deterministic random variables.

- $Y_n=x+1/n$: every term exceeds $x$, but $L=x$. Hence $B_x=\varnothing$ and $A_x=\Omega$.
- $Y_n=x$: every term equals $x$. Hence $A_x=\varnothing$ and $D_x=\Omega$.
- $Y_n=x-1/n$: every term is below $x$, but $L=x$. Hence $D_x=\varnothing$ and $C_x=\Omega$.

So all three differences arise at the boundary $L=x$. Away from that boundary the four events agree on membership. In particular, if $P(L=x)=0$, all four events have equal probabilities.

## 4. The three different positions of limsup in probability

For a fixed threshold $x$, consider

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_1(x)&=P(\limsup_n Y_n\geq x),\\
p_2(x)&=P(\limsup_n\{Y_n\geq x\}),\\
p_3(x)&=\limsup_n P(Y_n\geq x).
\end{aligned}
$$

The first takes the numerical limsup of the random variables along a fixed sample path, then asks whether that limsup is at least $x$.

The second asks whether the same realised sample point belongs to the threshold events infinitely often.

The third first computes a deterministic number for every $n$ (a marginal probability), and then takes the numerical limsup of these numbers. It is not itself an event.

The relationship is

$$
\boxed{p_1(x)\geq p_2(x)\geq p_3(x).}
$$

The first inequality follows from the set inclusion already proved. The second is Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*, 5th ed., Exercise 2.3.1, p. 58, with $A_n=\{Y_n\geq x\}$.

### Elementary proof using continuity from above

Let $A_n$ be arbitrary events and put

$$
F_N:=\bigcup_{n\geq N}A_n.
$$

The events $F_N$ decrease to $\limsup_n A_n$. For every $N$, $A_N\subseteq F_N$, hence $P(A_N)\leq P(F_N)$.

Taking the limsup of both sides,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\limsup_N P(A_N)
&\leq\limsup_N P(F_N)\\
&=\lim_{N\to\infty}P(F_N)\\
&=P(\limsup_n A_n).
\end{aligned}
$$

The ordinary limit on the right exists by monotonicity; the last equality is continuity from above, valid because $P(F_1)\leq1$ is finite. No independence is needed.

### Alternative proof using Fatou's lemma

Recall the indicator identity

$$
\mathbf1_{\limsup_n A_n}
=\limsup_n\mathbf1_{A_n}.
$$

This follows pointwise from the numerical limsup of a sequence taking only values zero and one: it is one exactly when infinitely many terms are one.

Write $U_n:=\mathbf1_{A_n}$. Since $0\leq U_n\leq1$, we can apply reverse Fatou's lemma:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\limsup_n A_n)
&=E[\limsup_n U_n]\\
&\geq\limsup_n E[U_n]\\
&=\limsup_n P(A_n).
\end{aligned}
$$

Even if we are only given ordinary Fatou's lemma for nonnegative random variables, we can derive the above very quickly. Apply it to $1-U_n\geq0$:

$$
E[\liminf_n(1-U_n)]
\leq\liminf_n E[1-U_n].
$$

Using $\liminf_n(1-U_n)=1-\limsup_n U_n$,

$$
1-E[\limsup_n U_n]
\leq1-\limsup_n E[U_n].
$$

Cancel the ones and reverse the inequality to obtain the desired result. All expectations here are finite because the indicators are bounded.

More generally, reverse Fatou holds when $U_n\leq Z$ a.s. for a common integrable upper bound $Z$. Nonpositivity itself is not necessary: apply ordinary Fatou to $Z-U_n\geq0$. On a probability space the constant one is a perfectly valid integrable upper bound for indicators.

## 5. Why the probability inequalities can be strict

The first gap between $p_1$ and $p_2$ can come from the boundary issue. Take $Y_n=x-1/n$. Then

$$
p_1(x)=1,\qquad p_2(x)=p_3(x)=0.
$$

The second gap between $p_2$ and $p_3$ is a different issue: marginal probabilities do not describe how often events occur along an infinite sample path.

For instance, let $Y_n$ be i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $1/2$, and take $x=1$. By the second Borel–Cantelli lemma,

$$
P(\limsup_n\{Y_n\geq1\})=1,
$$

while

$$
\limsup_n P(Y_n\geq1)=1/2.
$$

Hence $p_2(1)=1>p_3(1)=1/2$.

### Why we cannot replace the leftmost weak inequality by a strict one

Take $Y_n=x+1/n$. Then

$$
P(L>x)=0,\qquad
\limsup_n P(Y_n>x)=1.
$$

In the other direction, take i.i.d. Bernoulli$(1/2)$ random variables and $x=1/2$. By Borel–Cantelli, $L=1$ a.s., so

$$
P(L>x)=1,\qquad
\limsup_n P(Y_n>x)=1/2.
$$

These two examples also work if the marginal threshold is weak. Hence there is no universal ordering between $P(L>x)$ and either marginal limsup.

There is also no universal ordering between $P(\limsup_n\{Y_n>x\})$ and $\limsup_n P(Y_n\geq x)$. Taking $Y_n=x$ makes the former zero and the latter one; taking the Bernoulli example with $x=1/2$ makes the former one and the latter $1/2$.

In other words, the results at the top give a partial ordering of the probabilities, not a single chain containing all six of them.

## 6. Why this is useful in Durrett Exercise 3.4.2(a)

The original motivation was Durrett, 5th ed., Exercise 3.4.2(a), p. 127. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d., with $EX_1=0$ and $0<\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)<\infty$. Put

$$
S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n,\qquad
Y_n=\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}.
$$

The exercise asks us to use the CLT and Kolmogorov's zero-one law to show that

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}Y_n=+\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
$$

The CLT gives $Y_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2)$. Since the limiting normal distribution has no atoms, for every finite $x$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\limsup_n P(Y_n\geq x)
&=\lim_n P(Y_n\geq x)\\
&=1-\Phi(x/\sigma)>0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. The probability comparison therefore gives

$$
P(\limsup_n Y_n\geq x)
\geq\limsup_n P(Y_n\geq x)>0.
$$

The infinitely-often event is the bridge between marginal distribution information (from the CLT) and sample-path information (the numerical limsup).

The remaining task in the exercise is to justify the tail measurability needed for Kolmogorov's zero-one law and obtain the almost-sure conclusion for all thresholds. Importantly, although the increments $X_n$ are independent, the partial sums $S_n$ and the events $\{Y_n\geq x\}$ are not generally independent. We cannot just invoke the second Borel–Cantelli lemma on them.

## 7. Connection to almost-sure convergence

My original November 4 note used the nonnegative errors

$$
W_n=\lvert Y_n-Y\rvert,\qquad
Z=\limsup_n W_n.
$$

For every $\epsilon>0$ the inclusion chain gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{Z>\epsilon\}
&\subseteq\{W_n>\epsilon\text{ i.o.}\}\\
&\subseteq\{Z\geq\epsilon\}\\
&\subseteq\{Z>\epsilon/2\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For a fixed $\epsilon$ these events need not be equal, but the universally quantified statements are equivalent:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&[\forall\epsilon>0,\ 
P(W_n>\epsilon\text{ i.o.})=0]\\
&\qquad\iff
[\forall\delta>0,\ P(Z\leq\delta)=1].
\end{aligned}
$$

The threshold on one side need not be the same as the one on the other. This is the point behind Xiao Fang's qualification in the STAT5005 lecture notes.

Since $Z\geq0$, continuity from above along $\delta=1/k$ then gives $P(Z=0)=1$, which is equivalent to $Y_n\to Y$ a.s.

See the separate posts [Converges a.e. — Two Proofs of the Infinitely Often Characterisation](/durrett-waffling/almost-everywhere-convergence-two-proofs/) and [What Does an Event Occurring Infinitely Often Actually Mean?](/durrett-waffling/what-does-infinitely-often-mean/) for the detailed discussion.

## 8. Corresponding results for liminf (no proofs)

For completeness, here are the analogous results to keep as a reference. Write

$$
M:=\liminf_n Y_n=\sup_{N\geq1}\inf_{n\geq N}Y_n.
$$

### Four-event chain for lower thresholds

This is the direct dual of the limsup upper-threshold result:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{M<x\}
&\subseteq\limsup_n\{Y_n<x\}\\
&\subseteq\limsup_n\{Y_n\leq x\}\\
&\subseteq\{M\leq x\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here the middle events are still infinitely-often events. Equivalently, these are the limsup results applied to $-Y_n$.

The corresponding probability comparisons are

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(M\leq x)
&\geq P(\limsup_n\{Y_n\leq x\})\\
&\geq\limsup_n P(Y_n\leq x),
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(M\leq x)
&\geq P(\limsup_n\{Y_n<x\})\\
&\geq\limsup_n P(Y_n<x).
\end{aligned}
$$

### Four-event chain for set-theoretic liminf and upper thresholds

Here the middle events refer to eventual membership, not infinitely-often membership:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{M>x\}
&\subseteq\liminf_n\{Y_n>x\}\\
&\subseteq\liminf_n\{Y_n\geq x\}\\
&\subseteq\{M\geq x\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

All inclusions can be strict. Taking probabilities preserves the inclusions as inequalities.

The general event inequality is

$$
\boxed{P(\liminf_n A_n)\leq\liminf_n P(A_n).}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(M>x)
&\leq P(\liminf_n\{Y_n>x\})\\
&\leq\liminf_n P(Y_n>x),
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(M>x)
&\leq P(\liminf_n\{Y_n\geq x\})\\
&\leq\liminf_n P(Y_n\geq x).
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the numerical liminf event at the left uses a strict inequality in both cases.

Also, by monotonicity,

$$
\liminf_n P(Y_n>x)
\leq\liminf_n P(Y_n\geq x).
$$

For lower thresholds and set-theoretic liminf, the remaining dual chain is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{L<x\}
&\subseteq\liminf_n\{Y_n<x\}\\
&\subseteq\liminf_n\{Y_n\leq x\}\\
&\subseteq\{L\leq x\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(L<x)
&\leq P(\liminf_n\{Y_n<x\})\\
&\leq\liminf_n P(Y_n<x),
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(L<x)
&\leq P(\liminf_n\{Y_n\leq x\})\\
&\leq\liminf_n P(Y_n\leq x).
\end{aligned}
$$

### General identities for reference

$$
\limsup_n A_n
=\bigcap_{N=1}^{\infty}\bigcup_{n\geq N}A_n,
$$

$$
\liminf_n A_n
=\bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty}\bigcap_{n\geq N}A_n.
$$

$$
(\limsup_n A_n)^c=\liminf_n A_n^c,
$$

$$
(\liminf_n A_n)^c=\limsup_n A_n^c.
$$

$$
\mathbf1_{\limsup_n A_n}
=\limsup_n\mathbf1_{A_n},
$$

$$
\mathbf1_{\liminf_n A_n}
=\liminf_n\mathbf1_{A_n}.
$$

The two numerical definitions are

$$
\limsup_n Y_n=\inf_N\sup_{n\geq N}Y_n,
$$

$$
\liminf_n Y_n=\sup_N\inf_{n\geq N}Y_n,
$$

with $\liminf_n Y_n=-\limsup_n(-Y_n)$.

And the combined probability inequality for arbitrary events is

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\liminf_n A_n)
&\leq\liminf_n P(A_n)\\
&\leq\limsup_n P(A_n)\\
&\leq P(\limsup_n A_n).
\end{aligned}
$$

None of these general results requires independence or moment assumptions.

*References: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Section 2.3 and Exercise 2.3.1 (p. 58), Exercise 3.4.2(a) (p. 127); Xiao Fang, STAT5005 lecture notes, Chapter 2, Section 2.2, pp. 8–9.*
